title: Is AliExpress Legit & Safe to Use in Pakistan?
summary: Is AliExpress legit and safe in Pakistan? How buyer protection and disputes work, how to read a seller, customs, and the cash-on-delivery route.
body_markdown:
AliExpress is a legitimate company. It is the retail marketplace run by Alibaba Group, it has been trading for well over a decade, and Pakistani buyers order from it every day. The company is not the risk.


The risk is that AliExpress is a marketplace, not a shop. Thousands of independent sellers list on it, quality runs from excellent to worthless, and the platform's protection only helps if you use it inside its window. Pakistan also gets the harder version of the experience: payment up front by card, slow and variable delivery, customs that is not settled at checkout, and a return to China that rarely pays for itself.


So: safe to buy from if you pick sellers carefully, pay only on the platform, and keep orders small enough that a bad one is an annoyance rather than a loss. Below, how buyer protection works, how to read a seller, and the cash-on-delivery route to the same factories.


## Is AliExpress a real company?


Yes. AliExpress is part of Alibaba Group, one of the largest ecommerce groups in the world, and it is a genuine platform with a genuine payments and dispute system behind it. Orders are placed on the platform, the money is held rather than handed straight to the seller, and there is a formal process for opening a dispute if the parcel never arrives or arrives wrong.


That structure is the reason AliExpress is usable at all from Pakistan. It is also the reason every safety rule below comes down to the same thing: stay inside the platform, where that structure protects you.


## "Legit" and "safe" are two different questions


The platform being legitimate says nothing about the individual seller you are about to buy from. On a marketplace, risk sits at the listing level.


Three things vary seller by seller, and none of them are guaranteed by AliExpress itself: whether the product matches the photos and the specification, whether it ships when the seller says it will, and whether the seller responds when something is wrong. A store with years of trading history and thousands of orders behaves differently from a store opened last month, and the platform makes both visible to you before you pay.


The same logic applies to any marketplace, local or foreign. Our guide to[ordering from China safely](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/is-it-safe-to-order-from-china-pakistan) covers the general version, and[online shopping in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/cheapest-online-shopping-in-pakistan) puts every route to a Pakistani doorstep side by side.


## How AliExpress buyer protection actually works


Buyer protection is the part most people never read until they need it, and by then the clock has usually run out. The mechanics are simple enough:


- **Your money is held, not forwarded.** The seller is paid once the order completes, which is what gives a dispute any leverage at all.
- **Every order has a protection period.** It is shown on the order page, it counts down, and it ends. Check the date on your own order rather than assuming a standard length — it varies by seller and shipping method.
- **Disputes are opened on the platform.** Not over chat, not by email to the seller. If a seller asks you to close a dispute and promises to sort it out privately, you have just been asked to give up the only leverage you have.
- **Evidence decides the outcome.** Photographs of the parcel, the label and the item, and an unbroken unboxing video where the item is expensive. Take them before you throw the packaging away.
- **Never confirm receipt early.** Confirming a delivery you have not inspected releases the money and closes your window.


Partial refunds are common outcomes, and are often the sensible one: for a low-value item, agreeing a partial refund and keeping the product beats posting it back to China at your own cost.


## How to read an AliExpress seller before you pay


Most bad AliExpress orders were avoidable at the listing. Six checks, in the order they are worth doing:


- **Store age and order volume.** A store trading for years with a long order history has something to lose. A new store with a handful of sales does not.
- **The rating breakdown, not the headline score.** Look at how the item is scored on description accuracy specifically. That is the number that predicts whether the thing in the box matches the thing in the photo.
- **Buyer photo reviews.** These are the only images shot on the real product rather than lifted from the manufacturer. If every review photo looks like the listing photo, treat the reviews as decoration.
- **The specification, not the title.** Marketplace titles are keyword soup. Read the specification table for capacity, material, dimensions and version, then check the review text for people saying it arrived different.
- **Branded goods at implausible prices.** A well-known brand priced at a fraction of its usual price is not a deal. Cross-border marketplaces carry a great deal of counterfeit and grey stock, and a copy is the most likely explanation.
- **Shipping method and stated delivery window.** The cheapest shipping option is usually the slowest and the least trackable. Compare the total landed price and the delivery estimate, not the sticker.

## What is different for Pakistani buyers


AliExpress is a global platform with a local last mile that Pakistan is not the priority for. Five frictions come up again and again:


- **You pay before anything ships.** Cash on delivery is not an option, so the money leaves your account first and any recovery runs through a dispute. That is the single biggest difference from buying inside Pakistan.
- **Delivery is long and variable.** Cross-border parcels move through several handovers, and the difference between the cheap and the fast shipping option is measured in weeks, not days.
- **Customs is not settled at checkout.** Import charges on a cross-border parcel depend on the shipment, the declared value and the courier, so the price on the listing is not always the landed cost. Ask the courier for the paperwork if a charge appears, and factor the possibility in before you order.
- **Returns rarely pay.** Even when a seller accepts a return, the postage back to China usually costs more than the item. In practice a partial refund is the realistic remedy.
- **Support is remote.** Time zones, translated listings and chat-based support mean a problem takes days of back-and-forth rather than a phone call.


None of this makes the platform a scam. It makes it a platform where you should buy small, cheap and non-urgent things until you know a seller.[AliExpress vs Alibaba](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/aliexpress-vs-alibaba-pakistan) is worth reading if you are choosing between retail and wholesale routes, and[Temu in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/temu-in-pakistan-how-it-works-shipping-alternatives) covers the same trade-offs on the other big cross-border app.


## Payment safety: the rules that matter


Almost every serious loss on a cross-border marketplace involves payment leaving the platform. Four rules cover it:


- **Pay on the platform, always.** A seller asking for a bank transfer, an easypaisa payment or any off-platform method is asking you to drop buyer protection. There is no legitimate reason for the request.
- **Use a card you can control.** A card with a low limit, or a virtual card, keeps the downside bounded on a first order with a new seller.
- **Watch the currency conversion.** The rupee price you are quoted at checkout may not be the amount that lands on your statement once your bank's conversion is applied. Check the statement rather than the checkout screen.
- **Keep the order record.** Order number, screenshots, tracking and chat history. A dispute is decided on evidence, and the platform's chat log is part of it.


## What usually goes fine, and what usually goes wrong


After enough orders, a pattern shows up.


- **Usually fine:** cables, small tools, phone and laptop accessories, craft and hobby supplies, spare parts you can identify by model number, unbranded homeware. Low value, easy to specify, and a bad one costs little.
- **Mixed:** clothing and shoes (sizing is cut for a different market), anything colour-critical, cosmetics, and electronics where the internal specification is easy to misstate.
- **Usually a problem:** branded goods at implausible prices, anything with a battery or a plug where safety certification matters, fragile items on the cheapest shipping, and anything you need by a fixed date.

## A checklist before you press order


1. Check the store's age, order history and description-accuracy rating.
2. Read the specification table and three buyer photo reviews.
3. Compare the total with shipping, not the sticker price, and note the delivery window.
4. Pay on the platform, with a card you can limit. Never off-platform.
5. Note the protection window's end date on the order page the day it ships.
6. Film the unboxing for anything expensive, and keep the packaging until you are satisfied.
7. Open a dispute on the platform if something is wrong — before the window closes, not after.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is AliExpress a scam?


No. It is a legitimate marketplace owned by Alibaba Group, with a payments system that holds your money and a formal dispute process. Individual sellers on it can still be dishonest, which is why the seller checks above matter more than the platform's reputation.


### Does AliExpress deliver to Pakistan?


Yes, AliExpress ships to Pakistan, and delivery times vary widely by seller and shipping method. Cheaper shipping options take considerably longer and carry weaker tracking than paid express options.


### Can I use cash on delivery on AliExpress in Pakistan?


No. AliExpress takes payment up front, so cash on delivery is not available to Pakistani buyers. If paying before you see the product is the part you are uncomfortable with, Markaz China ships the same China catalogue on cash on delivery in rupees, in about 10–17 days.


### Will I have to pay customs duty on an AliExpress order in Pakistan?


It depends on the parcel, the declared value and the courier handling it, so treat any import charge as possible rather than certain and ask for the documentation if one appears. Buying through Markaz China avoids the question because freight and customs are handled door-to-door before the parcel reaches you.


### What do I do if my AliExpress order never arrives?


Open a dispute on the platform before the protection window on that order closes, and attach the tracking history. Do not let a seller talk you into closing the dispute on a promise — once it is closed, your leverage is gone.


### Are branded products on AliExpress genuine?


Assume not, unless the store is an authorised seller and the price is in the normal range for that brand. A recognisable brand at a fraction of its usual price is far more likely to be a copy than a bargain.


### Is AliExpress or a local Pakistani platform cheaper?


On sticker price, China-direct usually wins. On landed cost and speed, it is closer than it looks once shipping, waiting time and any import charges are counted. For anything urgent, local stock delivered in 3–5 days is normally the better buy.
